column2: On the authority of Ibn ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with them both), who said: The Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace) took hold of my shoulder and said:

“Be in this world as though you were a stranger or a wayfarer.” And Ibn ʿUmar (may Allah the Exalted be pleased with them both) used to say: “When evening comes, do not expect the morning; and when morning comes, do not expect the evening. Take from your health for your illness, and from your life for your death.” Reported by al-Bukhārī.
Bi-mankibī (“my shoulder”): with fatḥah on the mīm and kasrah on the kāf; where the upper arm meets the shoulder blade.
It is narrated both in the singular and in the dual.
“As though you were a stranger”: who finds no one to be at ease with and has no aim except to leave his exile for his homeland, without competing with anyone.

“Or a wayfarer”: one passing along the road, heading for his homeland. Aw (“or”) is in the sense of bal (“rather”), as a step up from the stranger, who may settle down in the land of his exile, to the wayfarer, who does not.
“Do not expect the morning”: [to do] the deeds of the night.
“Do not expect the evening”: because each of morning and evening has deeds particular to it which, if delayed, cannot be made up in full, even if making them up is prescribed.
“Take from your health for your illness”: seize the chance to do deeds while healthy, for an illness may come that prevents them, and you would arrive at the appointed time without provision.
“And from your life for your death”: do in your life what you will find of benefit after your death, for after death there is nothing but the cessation of deeds.
A teacher may touch the learner's limbs when teaching, to put him at ease and alert him.
Offering sincere advice and guidance to someone who has not asked for it.
Addressing one person while meaning everyone, for this does not apply only to Ibn ʿUmar; rather, it applies to the whole nation.
Urging people to leave this world and renounce it, and to take from it only the necessary amount that helps towards the Hereafter.

A warning against vices; for the stranger, knowing few people, has little envy, enmity, rancour, hypocrisy and quarrelling and all the vices that arise from mixing with people; and staying only a short while, he has few houses, gardens, farms and all the other things that distract from the Creator whoever Allah has not granted success.
Keeping one's hopes short and preparing for death.
Hastening to righteous deeds before one becomes unable to do them and illness, death or one of the signs after which no deed is accepted comes between.
